subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: You have been provided with three test tubes. One of them contains distilled water and the other two contain an acidic solution and a basic solution, respectively. If you are given only red litmus paper, how will you identify the contents of each test tube?
solution:
Red litmus is changed by only one of the three liquids, so the paper has to be used twice — once as supplied, and once after a base has converted it.

**Step 1 — find the base.** Dip a strip of red litmus paper into each of the three test tubes. It turns **blue** in only one of them, and that one holds the **basic solution**. The acid and the distilled water both leave red litmus unchanged, so this step cannot yet separate those two.

**Step 2 — use the blue paper the base has just made.** The strip that turned blue is now blue litmus. Dip it into each of the two remaining test tubes.

- The liquid that turns it **back to red** is the **acidic solution**.
- The liquid that leaves it **blue** is the **distilled water**, which is neutral and changes neither colour.
groundedIn: §2.1.1 Acids and Bases in the Laboratory, with Activity 2.1 and Table 2.1: red litmus turns blue in a base, blue litmus turns red in an acid, and a neutral liquid changes neither.

stem: Why should curd and sour substances not be kept in brass and copper vessels?
solution:
Curd and other sour foods are sour **because they contain acids** — curd holds lactic acid, tamarind tartaric acid, lemon and orange citric acid.

An acid reacts with a metal:

Acid + Metal \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Hydrogen gas

Brass and copper vessels are made of metal, so the acid in the food slowly eats into the vessel and forms **salts of copper and zinc**. These salts are toxic, and they also spoil the taste of the food. Curd is therefore stored in vessels the acid cannot attack, such as earthenware, glass or steel.
groundedIn: §2.1.2 How do Acids and Bases React with Metals? (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen) with Table 2.3, which names lactic acid in sour milk and citric, tartaric and oxalic acids in other sour foods.

stem: Which gas is usually liberated when an acid reacts with a metal? Illustrate with an example. How will you test for the presence of this gas?
solution:
**The gas is hydrogen.** A metal displaces the hydrogen of an acid and sets it free, leaving a salt behind:

Acid + Metal \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Hydrogen gas

**Example.** Zinc granules dropped into dilute sulphuric acid give off bubbles of hydrogen:

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

**Test.** Pass the gas through soap solution so that it collects in the bubbles, then bring a burning candle near a gas-filled bubble. The gas burns with a **pop sound**, which confirms hydrogen.
groundedIn: Activity 2.3 and Fig. 2.1, where zinc granules are treated with dilute sulphuric acid and the gas evolved is passed through soap solution and tested with a burning candle; the summary equation is in §2.1.2.

stem: Metal compound A reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce effervescence. The gas evolved extinguishes a burning candle. Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction if one of the compounds formed is calcium chloride.
solution:
Reading the three clues together:

- **Effervescence** with a dilute acid — a gas is being released, which points to a metal carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.
- The gas **extinguishes a burning candle** — it does not support combustion, so it is **carbon dioxide**.
- One product is **calcium chloride**, so the metal in compound A is calcium.

So **compound A is calcium carbonate**, \(\text{CaCO}_3\), and the balanced equation is:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §2.1.3 How do Metal Carbonates and Metal Hydrogencarbonates React with Acids? and Activity 2.5, which gives the general form: metal carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Why do HCl, HNO₃, etc., show acidic characters in aqueous solutions while solutions of compounds like alcohol and glucose do not show acidic character?
solution:
Acidic character is not a property of hydrogen in a compound — it is a property of hydrogen **released as \(\text{H}^+\) ions in water**.

\(\text{HCl}\) and \(\text{HNO}_3\) dissociate in water and produce \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions, which are what make a solution acidic:

\(\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)\)

Alcohol and glucose **also contain hydrogen**, but they do not ionise in water, so no \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions are produced. Their solutions therefore show no acidic character. This is exactly why the bulb glows for acid solutions but not for glucose or alcohol in the conductivity test — containing hydrogen is not the same as producing hydrogen ions.
groundedIn: Activity 2.8 (the bulb glows only for the acids) and §2.2 What do all Acids and all Bases have in Common?, which concludes that acids produce \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) in solution.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Why does an aqueous solution of an acid conduct electricity?
solution:
An acid dissociates in water to give **\(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions and the corresponding anion** — \(\text{Cl}^-\) from \(\text{HCl}\), \(\text{NO}_3^-\) from \(\text{HNO}_3\), and so on.

Electric current is carried through the solution by these **free ions**. Because an acid solution contains them and a solution of glucose or alcohol does not, the bulb glows for the acid and stays dark for the others.
groundedIn: Activity 2.8 with Fig. 2.3 and §2.2: the glowing bulb indicates a flow of current, and the electric current is carried through the acidic solution by ions.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Why does dry HCl gas not change the colour of the dry litmus paper?
solution:
Dry \(\text{HCl}\) gas has **no water to dissociate in**, so it does not produce \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions. Acidic behaviour — including turning blue litmus red — is shown by \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions, not by the molecule itself.

With dry gas and dry paper there is no moisture anywhere in the system, no ions are formed, and the litmus keeps its colour. Moisten the litmus paper (or the gas) and the colour change appears at once.
groundedIn: Activity 2.9 and §2.2.1 What Happens to an Acid or a Base in a Water Solution?, which establishes that an acid produces hydrogen ions only in the presence of water.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: While diluting an acid, why is it recommended that the acid should be added to water and not water to the acid?
solution:
Dissolving a concentrated acid in water is a **highly exothermic** process — a large amount of heat is released.

- **Acid added slowly to water (correct).** The water is present in bulk and absorbs the heat as it is released, so the temperature rises gradually and safely.
- **Water added to concentrated acid (dangerous).** The small amount of water released a great deal of heat in one place. The mixture can **splash out and cause burns**, and the glass container may **break from the excessive local heating**.

So the acid is always added to water, slowly and with constant stirring.
groundedIn: Activity 2.10 with Fig. 2.5 and §2.2.1, which states that the process is highly exothermic and warns that adding water to a concentrated acid may make the mixture splash out and may break the glass container.

stem: How is the concentration of hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) affected when a solution of an acid is diluted?
solution:
It **decreases**.

Diluting an acid does not destroy any hydronium ions, but it spreads the same number of them through a much larger volume of water. The **concentration — the number of \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\) ions per unit volume — therefore falls**, and the solution becomes less acidic (its pH rises towards 7).
groundedIn: §2.2.1, which defines dilution as mixing an acid or base with water resulting in a decrease in the concentration of \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+/\text{OH}^-\) ions per unit volume.

stem: How is the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH⁻) affected when excess base is dissolved in a solution of sodium hydroxide?
solution:
It **increases**.

A base dissolved in water produces \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) ions:

\(\text{NaOH}(s) \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{Na}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)\)

Adding more base to the solution therefore releases more hydroxide ions into the same volume, so the concentration of \(\text{OH}^-\) ions per unit volume goes up and the solution becomes more strongly alkaline.
groundedIn: §2.2.1, where bases are shown generating \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) ions in water, read with the dilution statement in the same section that concentration is measured per unit volume.

stem: You have two solutions, A and B. The pH of solution A is 6 and pH of solution B is 8. Which solution has more hydrogen ion concentration? Which of this is acidic and which one is basic?
solution:
On the pH scale, **the higher the hydrogen ion concentration, the lower the pH value**.

- **Solution A (pH 6) has the greater hydrogen ion concentration**, because its pH is the lower of the two.
- **Solution A is acidic** — its pH is less than 7.
- **Solution B is basic** — its pH is greater than 7.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which states that the pH of a neutral solution is 7, that values below 7 are acidic, and that higher the hydronium ion concentration, lower is the pH value; see also Fig. 2.6.

stem: What effect does the concentration of H⁺(aq) ions have on the nature of the solution?
solution:
The concentration of \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions is what **decides** whether a solution is acidic, neutral or basic.

- A **high** \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) concentration gives a **low pH** — the solution is **acidic**, and the higher the concentration the more strongly acidic it is.
- When the \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) concentration equals the \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) concentration the solution is **neutral**, pH 7.
- A **low** \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) concentration means \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) is in excess, the pH is above 7, and the solution is **basic**.
groundedIn: §2.3, which runs the pH scale from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline) and ties increasing pH above 7 to an increase in \(\text{OH}^-\) ion concentration; Fig. 2.6 shows both ion concentrations varying together.

stem: Do basic solutions also have H⁺(aq) ions? If yes, then why are these basic?
solution:
**Yes.** A basic solution still contains \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions — no aqueous solution is entirely free of them, which is why every solution can be placed somewhere on the pH scale rather than falling off it.

What makes such a solution basic is the **comparison between the two ions, not the absence of one of them**: in a basic solution the concentration of \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) ions is **greater than** the concentration of \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions. The excess of hydroxide ions is what gives the solution its basic nature and its pH above 7.
groundedIn: §2.3 with Fig. 2.6, which plots the variation of pH against the concentration of \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) **and** \(\text{OH}^-(aq)\) ions together, so both are present throughout the scale and it is their relative amounts that set the pH.

stem: Under what soil condition do you think a farmer would treat the soil of his fields with quick lime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) or chalk (calcium carbonate)?
solution:
A farmer would do this when the soil is **too acidic** — that is, when its pH has fallen below the range the crop needs for healthy growth.

Quick lime, slaked lime and chalk are all **basic** substances. Added to acidic soil they **neutralise the excess acid** and raise the pH back into the range the plants can tolerate.

The farmer would first test the pH of the soil, as in Activity 2.12, and treat it only if the test shows the soil is acidic.
groundedIn: §2.3.1 Importance of pH in Everyday Life (“What is the pH of the soil in your backyard?”), read with Activity 2.12, which tests soil pH; plants require a specific pH range for healthy growth.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: What is the common name of the compound CaOCl₂?
solution:
\(\text{CaOCl}_2\) is commonly called **bleaching powder**.

It is made by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime, and although it is written as \(\text{CaOCl}_2\) its actual composition is quite complex.
groundedIn: §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Bleaching powder”, which states that bleaching powder is represented as \(\text{CaOCl}_2\).

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: Name the substance which on treatment with chlorine yields bleaching powder.
solution:
**Dry slaked lime — calcium hydroxide, \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\).**

\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaOCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The chlorine used here is itself a product of the chlor-alkali process, in which electricity is passed through brine.
groundedIn: §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Bleaching powder”: bleaching powder is produced by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: Name the sodium compound which is used for softening hard water.
solution:
**Washing soda — sodium carbonate decahydrate, \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}\).**

It is obtained by recrystallising the sodium carbonate got from heating baking soda, and one of its listed uses is removing the permanent hardness of water.
groundedIn: §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Uses of washing soda”, item (iv): it is used for removing permanent hardness of water.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: What will happen if a solution of sodium hydrocarbonate is heated? Give the equation of the reaction involved.
solution:
On heating, sodium hydrogencarbonate **decomposes** to sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide:

\(2\text{NaHCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\)

This is the reaction that takes place when baking soda is heated during cooking. The carbon dioxide released is what makes bread and cake rise and turn soft and spongy.
groundedIn: §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Baking soda”, which gives the heating equation and notes the reaction that takes place when it is heated during cooking.

stem: Write an equation to show the reaction between Plaster of Paris and water.
solution:
Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate. On mixing with water it takes up water of crystallisation and changes back into gypsum, setting into a hard solid mass:

\(\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The half water molecule in the formula is written that way because **two formula units of \(\text{CaSO}_4\) share one molecule of water**.
groundedIn: §2.4.4 Are the Crystals of Salts really Dry?, under “Plaster of Paris”, which gives this equation and explains the half water molecule.
